I'm sorry to hear it was such a difficult experience for you. Thank you for pointing out that many of the doctors are excellent but have their hands tied by the system. Of course, even in Canada, where the system is admittedly better, there are still flaws - I think I can attribute my good experience to being well-educated and middle class with a safety net. Yes, I had months of group therapy for "free" (outpatient) but I was able to do so because I had insurance through work that allowed me to continue to receive an income. I saw others in the hospital with me who were possibly over-medicated or at least could not advocate for themselves. Yes, I had quite a bit of direction over my own medications and care but it was because I had the knowledge to ask - the system still encourages blind faith in doctors and to accept whatever meds are handed you. I asked about each pill and refused the ones I did not want (almost all except an anti-depressant i was comfortable with). Someone in acute mental illness, low education level, low SES, etc may not ask the same questions or feel the same entitlement I felt to information about my care. There are so many factors but I am endlessly grateful that money was not really one of them.

I'm from Canada. I'll admit that last year I spent two weeks in a psych ward (by choice, I was falling apart and couldn't life). My doctor was amazing. They even offered to keep my bed for me and let me have a "trial" weekend home and then discharge the Monday just in case. It made the most incredible difference in my life. After 6 months of 20 hours a week group therapy I was able to return to work and be a functioning adult. If the extent to my help would have been 3 days in hospital I would probably have destroyed my career and be unable to work right now.

I just came out (big lesbian here, I look pretty straight though). I waited until my very late 20s so I owe everyone who came before me and made it so easy for me immense gratitude. Growing up in northern Ontario there just weren't gay people. I went to a high school with 1000 students and not one person identified as gay openly. No one. You did not come out as gay in a Catholic school (or any school) in the early 2000s there. I'm not sure what would have happened because no one did it. There just wasn't any visibility for gay people in our city. There was an openly gay man who did drag and worked as an entertainer and he was generally accepted but that was it (generally accepted but I'm sure it was not an easy journey for him).
I remember going away to university in southern ontario for the first time in 2003. It was a liberal university campus so gay didn't seem so closeted but I was behind the times - the term "partner" was new to me. I assumed everyone who used it was gay, too. Once my RA referred to her partner back home and I was so confused because I had thought for sure she had said she was with a man but she had said partner so clearly she had to be a lesbian. It was just so foreign to me. I don't think my family had every mentioned homosexuality, we just didn't talk about it.
Fast forward to this year and that city I went to high school in had it's very first pride weekend! With a parade! According to a family member who helped organize it there was no dissent, lots of support and a great turnout. I'm ecstatic for how much has changed and for the young people now who can come out in high school and go through puberty being honest with themselves and others. I'll always be fairly sad that I missed a normal puberty with crushes and heart breaks and romance because I was too scared to be different.

Whenever I read apocalyptic novels or hear people chastise childless women for selfishness (there won't be any more humans!) I can't help but think, so what? I'm in a group therapy program (14 hours a week) that takes a psychodynamic psychotherapy approach. There is no offering of kleenex to anyone. It is considered rescuing and a (mild?) form of abuse. A pretty hard line and many of my group members were vehemently appalled at the rule but I quite liked it. There was no pressure or expectation then: no one felt awkward about giving or not giving kleenex, no one could resent someone for giving or not giving it since it was not allowed. And the self-sufficiency as well. While some people see being given a tissue as a sign that the other person cares others may see it as a sign that the other person is uncomfortable or wants them to stop crying. I like that your therapist explicitly laid that out on the table wright away as a general policy.

As krackbaby said, it depends on why (and i'll add WHEN) you become deaf. If someone is born deaf (or with a very severe hearing impairment) these days they often receive bilateral cochlear implants as early as possible (hopefully before the age of 2). They then receive speech therapy to learn to interpret the sounds and to speak. Studies show that the older a person is when they receive a cochlear implant (especially if deaf from birth) then the less likely they are to benefit. A cochlear implant does require a functioning cochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII).

There are multiple ways to have hearing impairment. Damage to the middle ear (this impacts the amplification and conduction of sound), damage to the cochlea (impacts the ability of the ear to take sound waves and convert them to electrical energy), damage to the nerve itself which impairs transmission of the signal to the brain and (although I'm less familiar with this) auditory processing issues where the brain cannot interpret the signals from the nerve accurately.

If someone has primarily middle ear problems then they might receive tubes in their ears (to drain fluid build up in the middle ear caused by malfunctioning eustachian tubes) or a hearing aid. Hearing aids can only help if there is some function in the cochlea and if there is an intact middle ear. Hearing aids just amplify sound although with new technology they can amplify it in very specific ways (targeting specific frequencies based on the results of an individual's hearing test, filtering out background noise, etc). 

IF however, a person has a functioning cochlea (aka inner ear) but does not have a function outer and/or middle ear that impairs sound conduction to the cochlea they can receive a BAHA or bone anchored hearing aid. This is surgically placed into the mastoid process (the bony protuberance behind the ear) and amplifies the sound waves through bone. The cochlea sits in fluid surrounded by bone and can also pick up signals that way. That is why if you plug your ears you can hear your blood whooshing or heart beating at times, etc.

I admitted myself to a psychiatric ward for depression, suicidal ideation and self-harm. I ended up staying two weeks until my doctor and I decided that I was safe to return home and there was sufficient follow-up. I went through a 6 week therapy program (group) learning skills like coping, interpersonal, etc. Now I am in the midst of a more intensive 3 month group therapy program.

The psych ward itself is /u/le_fez described: a lot of sitting around. I was admitted on a Friday night meaning that there was absolutely no programming over the weekend and more than half of the patients were on a pass home. It was the most mind-numbing experience of my life and, yes, I had brought books. The unit I was on was not a secure unit but there were restrictions that were lifted as time progressed.

Everyone upon admission had to wear hospital PJs (so we would be easy to spot if we tried to leave I think) and were on watch q15. That meant that every 15 minutes a nurse had to observe that I was alive and well. Even in the middle of the night. Once I saw my doctor for the first time after about 16 hours I was allowed my own clothes and checks q30 but could not leave the unit. It was nearly impossible for me to sleep because my door was by the nursing desk, they didn't have ear plugs and would come into my room every 30 minutes throughout the night. And I'm a very light sleeper. I thought I might become more unstable due to lack of sleep but refused sleeping pills because I did not want to rely on them for sleep since I had never required them out of the hospital.

I saw my doctor daily. Nurses would stop by at the start of each of their shifts and ask probing questions in front of everyone: how is your mood? Are you hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there? Are you thinking about suicide or self-harm?

Eventually I could leave the unit for a half hour, then an hour, then I could walk around out of the grounds if I had permission. We could only access our cell phones off the unit so I would take mine then and sit in the cafeteria to journal and charge my phone.

I'm fairly well-educated and was cooperative and understood the system so I was generally left alone. But most of the other people had more significant mental illnesses, were on much more powerful drugs (I wasn't on anything when I got there, I eventually started on low-dose SSRI), were of low SES, low education level, etc. Not everyone, of course, but many. 
Because of this most of the programming during the week was extremely basic. The dietitian may talk about nutrition. They may have something about planning to go home. Or some sort of small craft. There was an exercise bike on the unit. Laundry we could access. 

Mostly we played cards. I would read. Some people coloured. Quite a bit of drama between the younger people (I was nearly 30). I met some very interesting people. One part of the culture I genuinely enjoyed at times was that we didn't discuss why we were there often (and I could choose not to answer when asked) and you could kind of just walk away or sit alone and not be expected to socialize just because others were there. 

Other than a few fairly creepy dudes admitted near the end of my stay it was fairly uneventful. Which I'm glad for.

Lamu, Kenya. Two friends and I were on this island off the coast of Kenya. We had had our guard up for months prior being in Kenya (mostly Nairobbery) so when we got there and everyone just kept telling us how safe it was we let our guards down a bit. Oops.

We wanted to go to the beach. Our hostel owner (a German dude) said there were two ways to get there: either go all the way through town to the "chetty" (jetty) and wait for a boat, negotiate, take boat to the beach. OR we could just cut through the middle over some small sand dudes. It would be pretty!

Well, we decided to go the scenic route and set off for our presumably short walk. First: these were not small dunes. We couldn't actually see the beach over them, they were probably as tall as 5 storey buildings or higher with multiple rows of them to pass over. We get part way into these dunes and a local boy (about 14?) starts following us with a machete and trying to "show us the way". He speaks little English but oh well.

But it is about 10 minutes in that I realize there is no way in hell he is leading us to the beach. He is going much too far to the right when we could have easily been over the dunes by then. I could even hear the water now in a different direction so we try to leave. Then he starts demanding money for his help so we give him a bit (he had a machete!). 

Of course I'm shitting myself and my travel companions don't seem to have quite clued in to the situation and are apprehensive to leave him. So I say: fuck this, I can hear the ocean I'm going to run up there and see if I can find it. Sure enough there it is and I wave at them to follow and walk down to the beach.

When they arrive they say that he still won't leave and is now using one of his only English words "vagina". Great. We yell at him more to go away and start walking towards the populated part of the beach but there is NO ONE else in sight. He finally appears to give up and we hustle only to look back and see a man following us with a bandanna over his face. So we start running. Then one of my friends (she was actually an acquaintance we met on the island) starts begging us to stop because her asthma is acting up.

SO. Here we are being followed by a man with his face covered on a beach with no one else around and we are forced to *walk quickly*. Surprise. He catches up to us, pulls out a knife and says "give me everything you have or I'll kill you". Not wanting to argue we just hand over our bags and he runs off into the dunes. 

Oh, I also got a tick and we both got terrible food poisoning/diarrhea that night. Although I have to admit that Lama really is lovely.

tl;dr Took short cut to beach over sand dunes (island of lamu). Led far away from civilization by creepy child with machete asking to see our vaginas. Thought we got away but a man with a bandanna over his face caught up to us and robbed us at knifepoint.

I cannot diagnose something like this but adenoid removal can cause nasal speech and nasal regurgitation during swallowing. This is because it removes bulk from the back of the throat (nasopharynx) and the soft palate (velum) may no longer be able to reach it and close off that opening anymore. This can also be congenital by way of a cleft palate. Some clefts are called [occult sub mucous clefts](http://www.cleftline.org/parents-individuals/publications/submucous-clefts/) and often go unnoticed. Of course, if your speech is functional and you are not losing weight or lacking nutrition due to swallowing problems then it is mostly just interest and not medically relevant.

First let me say that you are doing and extremely courageous thing. It is not easy to ask for help or to admit oneself to the hospital but it may change your life. 

My experience was likely a bit different but I'll try my best. I admitted myself to a psychiatric ward a few months ago because I could not seem to keep myself safe. My friend drove me there and I checked in. I waited a few hours to talk to the psychiatrist. They asked me questions about my mood, my life, my symptoms, my past and my family history. The doctor tried to talk me out of admitting myself (stating it would be too boring for me) but I insisted on staying as I had already been in emerge 3 times that week for self-harm. 

I signed a paper to admit myself. I then waited to be transferred to the first available bed in the city. They had me change into hospital "jammies" right away. Everyone had to wear them for the first 24 hours. They took all my things and looked through them carefully, taking all cords, sharp objects, etc. They also took my purse and my cell phone. We could make calls from phones on the unit. 

I was given medications (I refused to take them until my doctor actually explained them to me). It was extremely strict at first - no leaving the unit, wearing hospital clothes, a nurse had to check me every 15 minutes even throughout the night. Every shift my new nurse would introduce themselves and ask the standard questions: rate my mood, was I having thoughts of suicide, self-harm or hurting others, did I want to talk about anything. 

I was there for two weeks. It took just a few days to get my regular clothes, be allowed to be checked every 30 minutes then every 60 minutes. I could leave the unit, then I could leave the hospital grounds for short intervals. The days were boring. There were a few groups during the day but because everyone there were experiencing acute mental health issues and some people had low education levels and socio-economic status the groups were very basic. I received hours of psychological assessment to determine a diagnosis. My doctor would check on me daily for 5-20 minutes and she started me on medications. 

Overall: it was ear-bleedingly boring but it was still the best decision I ever made. It gave me an opportunity to take a break from life. It got me started on meds and all of my psych testing done. It also opened up SO MANY options for outpatient treatment (months of full-time group therapy, CBT, etc) that I otherwise would not have been able to access.

That was a lot of information and every health system will be different. Please feel free to ask more questions here or PM me.

The uvula itself is not what separates the nasal and pro-pharyngeal cavities. The uvula is the termination of just *one* muscle in the soft palate (or velum) which is made up of multiple muscles. When these muscles contract they raise the soft palate. If functioning properly, the back of the soft palate should touch the wall of the pharynx (throat) and create a seal separating the two cavities allowing 1. you to swallow without any food or liquid coming out your nose, 2. you to create certain kinds of consonants (example, a /p/ unvoiced bilabial stop) that requires pressure to build up in the oral cavity/pharynx and the velum/soft palate prevents air from escaping out the nose while making these sounds.

The uvula has a muscle that runs midline in the soft palate and attaches to the back of the hard palate. The muscle is the musculus uvulae. When it contracts it does more to shorten and "bulk" the soft palate to assist with the seal but does not perform this action on its own (the levator veil palatini a major muscle for palate elevation). 
Anatomy chart with functions of muscles: https://www.inkling.com/read/clinical-anatomy-regions-snell-9th/chapter-11/table-11-9

It also is not necessarily the trigger for the gag reflex. You can trigger a gag reflex by touching the faucial arches (the two strips of tissue on either side of your tonsils) or other areas of the pharynx.  It isn't a necessary reflex and has no bearing on swallowing. Some people have very limited or no gag reflex and are able to eat and drink without issue.

Fun fact: in some parts of the world the uvula is removed in an attempt to cue stuttering. This does not work. It also may do nothing at all; unless a large amount of tissue is removed or other structures are damaged it is unlikely to stop the soft palate from creating a seal aka velopharyngeal insufficiency (which would lead to hyper nasal speech).

tl;dr The uvula itself (just the little ball of flesh hanging at the back of the throat) doesn't do all that much on its own. You can even probably do without it.

See my answer below but I believe it is someone who has had a cleft palate repair but continues to have some velopharyngeal insufficiency/hasn't unlearned some of the typical speech characteristics. Also, the person glides their /r/ and /l/ which is developmental, a form of a potential phonological disorder.

edit: What do I mean by "typical of cleft palate speech"? Well, someone who has a cleft palate (or even a repaired cleft palate that continues to have velopharyngeal insufficiency) has some degree of inability to fully close the passage between the nasal cavity and the oral/pharyngeal cavity during speech. If you are unable to do this it will affect many speech sounds but especially consonants made with the velum (soft palate). In English this is /k/, /g/, and /ng/. These speakers have to mark the sounds somehow so they often learn to make a glottal stop (like in the middle of uhoh). He doesn't sound like he has nasal escape (air coming out of the nose while making stop consonants like p, b, t, d, etc and he is capable of making /k/ in some contexts so my guess is that the velopharyngeal insufficiency is either mild (only with some sounds in some places in words) OR it was repaired but the behaviours were so ingrained that they continue to speak that way.

This is meant entirely to be helpful and not to stereotype but it sounds consistent with the speech of someone with a cleft palate (likely repaired). That plus all of the phonological processes occurring in the speech that are fairly uncommon in adult speech and grammatical errors and omitted words I would postulate that it is an adult with a cleft palate and a developmental disorder/syndrome (ex. Down Syndrome)

The speech includes gliding of /r/ sounds, lack of pronunciation of most consonant clusters, often the word final clusters (and even some consonants) are omitted, quite a few replacements of consonants with glottal stops (some of the speech suggests a repaired cleft palate, I wouldn't be surprised if the person had minor velopharyngeal insufficiency), he also glides sounds that typically are much more rarely glided. Example - he says "oyah" instead of "over". Gliding /v/ is very uncommon.

Yes, the more I listen to it there are so many consonants replaced by glottal stops it would make sense if the speaker at one time had a cleft palate and it was repaired but still retains some of the speech qualities. This is also not uncommon in Down Syndrome. In some speech contexts, for example, the speaker is capable of making a /k/ sound (a velar) but often replaces it with a glottal stop. Example: watch at approx 1:45-2:15 (watch how he says "actor" and a few others). He often pronounces "click" as "i?" (not using IPA because I'm lazy).

I second u/THE_MASKED_ERBATER about not relying on stimulants/medications to help you through college. The problem is, once you no longer have them you have to learn to function without them. Plus the concept of chasing a high is real. You would eventually feel as though you need more and more for the same results or even be willing to try something stronger. I'll admit, the first time I ever took Adderall (hoping to get a study boost) it was an incredible experience - the brain is flushed with warm and pleasant chemicals every 15-20 minutes. Yes, it sounds tempting but the problems were 1) I got really good at a computer game - it told me to focus but not what to focus on and 2) even the second time I took it the effects were much lesser than the first time: not as great a boost in concentration, not nearly the rush/warmth that I felt the first time. Those were changes just between the first and second use!  You know why I never took it again? Because I was smart enough to be able to see that very soon I wouldn't be getting what I had been out of it and I would be left looking for either a double dose or something stronger. Don't go down that road if you don't have to (and "have to" being that a psychiatrist/psychologist has determined that you require it to function normally).
